# Code review iteration

Reviewed the whole `go.octolab.org` module at commit `22a5242 2022-03-09`: all 93 Go files across `async`, `encoding`, `env`, `errors`, `exp`, `fn`, `io`, `pointer`, `runtime`, `safe`, `sequence`, `sort`, `strings`, `sync`, `testing`, `time`, `unsafe`, plus `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `Makefile`, `.golangci.yml`, and `.github/` CI configuration (workflows, dependabot, probot files). The review angle is a return-to-maintenance audit: real defects first, then idiomaticity against Go 1.26-era practice, then a judgment on whether each package still deserves to exist now that generics, `slices`, `cmp`, and newer stdlib APIs cover most of this ground. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps. No previous files existed in `.github/reviews/`, so all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. RepeatableReadCloser treats any short read as end of stream

`io/io.go:107-118`

```go
eof = n == 0 && errors.Is(err, io.EOF)
eof = eof || (n < len(p) && err == nil) // danger zone ("repeatable request")
```

The second line violates the `io.Reader` contract: a reader is explicitly allowed to return `n < len(p)` with a nil error in the middle of a stream — network bodies, `bufio` at buffer boundaries, and chunked HTTP readers do this routinely. When that happens, `repeatable.Read` declares EOF, rotates its buffer, and returns `io.EOF` to the caller. Two consequences: the consumer sees a truncated payload, and the replay buffer is rotated with only the bytes read so far, so every subsequent "repeat" replays the truncated prefix. Silent data corruption on retried requests — exactly the use case the type advertises. The tests only exercise `strings.Reader`, `bytes.Reader`, and a small file, which all fill the buffer in one call, so the defect is invisible to the suite. The `// danger zone` comment shows the author knew this was a gamble.

**Fix.** Rotate only on a genuine `io.EOF` (including the `n > 0 && err == io.EOF` form, which the first condition also misses on the same call). Since the whole point is replaying a fully known payload, a simpler and correct design is to slurp the source once and hand out `bytes.Reader`s that `Seek(0)` on rotation — no heuristics needed. Also consider satisfying `http.Request.GetBody` instead, which is the mechanism `net/http` actually uses for retries and redirects.

## 2. Classifier matches errors with inverted errors.Is semantics

`errors/classifier.go:27-39` (and the same pattern at `errors/classifier.go:53-54`)

```go
for class, list := range classifier {
    for _, target := range list {
        if errors.Is(target, err) {
```

`errors.Is(err, target)` is the standard direction: walk err's chain and consult err's own `Is` methods. This code calls it backwards, so the `Is` methods of *registered errors* are consulted and the `Is` methods of *incoming errors* never are. Concrete failure: `classifier.ClassifyAs("fs", os.ErrNotExist)` then `Classify(err)` where `err` is a `syscall.ENOENT` from a real syscall. `errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)` is true via `Errno.Is`, but `errors.Is(os.ErrNotExist, ENOENT)` is false — the error lands in `unknown`. The inversion is deliberate (the bundled `MessageError`/`NetworkError` matchers implement `Is(err)` in the reversed direction), but it silently breaks classification for every error that follows the stdlib convention, i.e. most of the ecosystem. Compounding it, `Classify` first collapses `err` to its root via `Unwrap` (line 28), so intermediate wrapper types can never match either.

**Fix.** Match in both directions against the original, un-collapsed error: `errors.Is(err, target) || errors.Is(target, err)`. That keeps the existing matcher types working while restoring standard sentinel behavior. Drop the pre-`Unwrap` — `errors.Is` already walks the chain (including `Unwrap() []error` trees, which the local `Unwrap` cannot traverse, see [[#8. Unwrap shadows the stdlib name with different semantics and ignores joined errors]]).

## 3. Toolchain and CI are frozen in early 2022 and partially broken

`go.mod:3`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.golangci.yml`, `tools/go.mod`, `Makefile:5`

Single consolidated staleness finding; everything below is one modernization effort.

- `go 1.13` directive: the module still compiles under old *language semantics* — per-iteration loop variables (Go 1.22) do not apply, and `panic(nil)` detection (Go 1.21) is disabled via the `panicnil` GODEBUG derived from this directive. This is not just cosmetic.
- Dependencies: `github.com/pkg/errors` (archived Dec 2021 — stdlib wrapping replaced it), `github.com/golang/mock` (archived June 2023 — the maintained fork is `go.uber.org/mock`), `github.com/google/uuid` v1.3.0 (v1.6+ adds UUIDv7), `gofakeit/v6` (v7 is current), `testify` v1.8.3 (v1.11+).
- CI is hard-broken today: `actions/upload-artifact@v3` / `download-artifact@v3` were shut off by GitHub on 2025-01-30, so the `report` job cannot run at all. `checkout@v3`, `setup-go@v4`, `cache@v3` are one-to-two majors behind. The test matrix tops out at Go 1.19 (EOL 2023); `Makefile:5` pins `GO_VERSIONS = 1.11 ... 1.19`.
- Lint: `tools/go.mod` pins golangci-lint v1.51.0 through personal forks (`kamilsk/golangci-lint`, `kamilsk/go-tools` replaces) — unauditable and stuck. golangci-lint v2 changed the config schema (`linters: fast:` is gone), and `exportloopref` (`.golangci.yml:17`) is deprecated, removed in v2, and moot once the go directive reaches 1.22.
- Probot-era configs: `.github/stale.yml` and `.github/settings.yml` drive apps that are effectively dead (the stale config itself links the deprecation issue); `actions/stale` and repository rulesets are the replacements. `.github/dependabot.yml:22-24` registers an npm ecosystem for `/docs/`, a directory that does not exist.
- No `govulncheck`, no CodeQL/scorecard job.
- Code-level era markers: `io/ioutil` (`io/io.go:7`, `testing/content.go:4`) deprecated since Go 1.16; `interface{}` throughout instead of `any` (Go 1.18).

**Fix.** One migration PR: bump `go` directive to a supported version (1.24+ as of today), swap `pkg/errors` for `fmt.Errorf("%w")`+`errors.Join`, `golang/mock` for `go.uber.org/mock`, `ioutil` for `io`/`os`, `interface{}` for `any`. Rebuild CI on current majors (`checkout@v5`, `setup-go@v6` with built-in caching — the separate `actions/cache` block is redundant, `upload-artifact@v4`), matrix of the two supported Go versions only, add `govulncheck` and dependabot-driven action bumps. Move lint to upstream golangci-lint v2 with a rewritten config; delete the fork replaces. Delete `stale.yml`/`settings.yml` or port to maintained equivalents.

## 4. SetEnvs holds a global mutex across the test body and deadlocks on failure

`testing/env.go:49, 68, 80-89`

`setEnvs` takes the package-level `guard.Lock()` and the only `Unlock` lives in the returned `rollback` closure. The lock is therefore held from `SetEnvs` until the caller invokes `release`. If the test fails in between — and the documented usage is exactly that: `require.NoError`/`assert.Equal` between the two calls, where `require` triggers `runtime.Goexit` — `release` is never called and every subsequent `SetEnvs` in the whole test binary blocks forever with no diagnostic. A forgotten `release` does the same. A test helper whose failure mode is "the rest of the suite hangs" is a trap. Additionally, with duplicated variable names in `vars`, `before` records the intermediate value on the second pass (line 71-72), so rollback restores the wrong original.

**Fix.** Delete the package: `t.Setenv` (Go 1.17) does scoped set-and-restore, integrates with the testing framework, and correctly panics when combined with `t.Parallel` instead of pretending parallel env mutation is safe. If a non-`testing.T` variant must stay, make release a `t.Cleanup`-style function registered before any assertion can run, and never let a user-visible code path decide whether a global mutex gets unlocked.

## 5. Watcher panic recovery unlocks a mutex it may not hold and dies silently

`async/watcher.go:52-55`

```go
}, func(err error) {
    watcher.guard.RUnlock()
    watcher.Stop()
})
```

The error handler compensates for a panic escaping a callback inside the `RLock` critical section (there is no `defer RUnlock` in the loop, so the lock is indeed left held). That coupling is invisible and fragile: the handler fires for *any* non-nil error from the `safe.Do` body, and only one specific panic site happens to hold the read lock. Any future change — a panic in `Stop`, a callback map refactor, an early `return err` — turns this into `sync: RUnlock of unlocked RWMutex`, which is itself an unrecoverable panic inside a goroutine. Beyond fragility: one panicking callback permanently kills the watcher for all other registered callbacks, the panic value in `err` is discarded (never logged, never surfaced), `Start` cannot be called again because the `sync.Once` is consumed, and the constructor's ticker leaks if `Start` is never invoked. The test suite acknowledges the instability: `async/watcher_test.go:36` carries `// TODO:fix unexpected data race`. Smaller API points: `Watcher` returns the unexported `*watcher` (`async/watcher.go:11`), stores a `context.Context` in a struct field, and `time.NewTicker` panics on a non-positive `frequency`.

**Fix.** Put the recovery where the risk is: wrap each callback invocation in its own `safe.Do` (or an inline `defer recover()`), use `defer watcher.guard.RUnlock()` around the iteration, and surface callback panics through an injectable error handler instead of dropping them. Copy the callback list under the lock and invoke it after unlocking to decouple callback latency from `Watch`/`Forget`. Return an exported type, accept the ticker lazily in `Start`, and validate `frequency`.

## 6. Caller resolves PCs with FuncForPC which is wrong under inlining

`runtime/caller.go:20-24`

```go
pc := make([]uintptr, 1)
runtime.Callers(2, pc)
f := runtime.FuncForPC(pc[0])
file, line := f.FileLine(pc[0])
```

Three defects in four lines. (a) The return value of `runtime.Callers` is ignored; if it is 0, `FuncForPC(0)` returns nil and `f.Name()` panics. (b) The `runtime.Callers` documentation explicitly forbids this pattern: the returned PCs must go through `runtime.CallersFrames`, because `FuncForPC` cannot account for inlining — and with today's more aggressive mid-stack inlining (Go 1.20+), a caller compiled at `go 1.13` semantics in 2022 rarely got inlined, but the same code built with a modern toolchain will misattribute names to the outermost inlined function. (c) `pc[0]` is a *return address*, so `FileLine` reports the line after the call, an off-by-one that `CallersFrames` handles internally.

**Fix.** `n := runtime.Callers(2, pc[:]); if n == 0 { return CallerInfo{} }; frame, _ := runtime.CallersFrames(pc[:n]).Next()` and take `frame.Function`, `frame.File`, `frame.Line`. The regex-based `Meta` parser (`runtime/caller.go:35-48`) should also be revisited against generic function name mangling (`Foo[...]`), which did not exist when it was written.

## 7. UUID.Next swallows randomness failures and returns a stale value

`sequence/generator/uuid.go:19-25`

```go
func (generator UUID) Next() UUID {
    id, err := uuid.NewRandom()
    if err != nil {
        return generator
    }
    return UUID(id)
}
```

On a randomness failure this returns the receiver — for the documented usage `new(generator.UUID)` that is the zero UUID, whose `String()` is `""`; in a loop it means silently repeated identifiers. An ID generator that can return duplicates or empties on error, with no signal whatsoever, is worse than one that panics: the docstring even shrugs, "may or may not be valid". If these IDs ever reach security-relevant contexts, silent degradation to a predictable value is a real hazard.

**Fix.** Follow `uuid.Must(uuid.NewRandom())` and panic — since Go 1.24 `crypto/rand.Read` is documented never to fail on supported platforms, so the panic branch is effectively dead anyway. Honestly, the whole type adds nothing over calling `github.com/google/uuid` directly (see [[#11. Most packages are superseded by the modern standard library]]); `Valid` also mislabels the nil UUID as invalid, which RFC 9562 does not.

## 8. Unwrap shadows the stdlib name with different semantics and ignores joined errors

`errors/errors.go:56-80`

The package positions itself as a drop-in for stdlib `errors` — `As` and `Is` are verbatim re-exports (`errors/proxy.go:21,38`) — but `Unwrap` is not: stdlib `errors.Unwrap` peels exactly one layer, this one loops to the root (pkg/errors' `Cause` semantics). Anyone switching an import between `errors` and `go.octolab.org/errors` silently changes behavior of the same-named function. Worse, the loop predates Go 1.20 multi-errors: a node wrapped via `errors.Join` or `fmt.Errorf` with two `%w` verbs implements `Unwrap() []error`, not `Unwrap() error`, so the walk stops there and "root cause" is simply the join node — in 2026 code that is a common shape, and `Classify` inherits the blindness because it roots every error through this function (`errors/classifier.go:28`).

**Fix.** Rename to something honest (`RootCause`), document that multi-error trees have no single root, and either return the join node explicitly or walk `Unwrap() []error` with a defined policy (first child, or all leaves). Better: stop pre-rooting errors entirely and lean on `errors.Is`/`errors.As`, which already traverse both chain shapes.

## 9. SignalTrap.Wait is single-use but nothing enforces it

`sync/signal.go:41-51`

`Wait` runs `defer close(trap)` and `defer signal.Stop(trap)`. Call it twice — or from two goroutines, a natural reading of "wait for termination" — and the second caller both (a) instantly gets a spurious `ErrSignalTrapped` because receiving from the closed channel succeeds with the zero value, and (b) panics with `close of closed channel` on its own deferred close. Nothing in the type or docs says single-shot. Also, `Termination` (`sync/signal.go:27`) registers `os.Interrupt` and `syscall.SIGINT`, which are the same signal, so a buffer of 3 holds duplicates.

**Fix.** The stdlib made this package obsolete: `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)` (Go 1.16) gives the same "block until signal or parent cancellation" contract with idempotent cancel semantics. If `SignalTrap` survives for API compatibility, guard the close with `sync.Once` and distinguish "signal" from "channel closed" by checking the received `ok` flag.

## 10. Exclude destroys its input slice without documenting it

`strings/filter.go:3-19`

```go
func Exclude(from []string, what ...string) []string {
    filtered := from[:0]
```

`Exclude` reuses the input's backing array. After `kept := strings.Exclude(all, "x")`, the caller's `all` is corrupted — its prefix is overwritten by the filtered result while its length still covers stale tail elements. The sibling functions `NotEmpty` and `Unique` at least say "in-place" in their doc comments; `Exclude` has no doc comment at all, so the mutation is a pure landmine for the exported API of a utility library.

**Fix.** Document the aliasing loudly or allocate a fresh slice. The real 2026 answer is `slices.DeleteFunc(from, func(s string) bool { return slices.Contains(what, s) })`, where the stdlib name and docs carry the in-place contract for you — see [[#11. Most packages are superseded by the modern standard library]].

## 11. Most packages are superseded by the modern standard library

`docs.go:1` (module-wide judgment, requested review angle)

This module was a rational grab-bag for Go 1.13. Generics (1.18), `slices`/`maps` (1.21), `cmp` (1.21/1.22), range-over-int (1.22), and newer runtime APIs have since absorbed most of it. Package-by-package:

| Package                              | Verdict     | Superseded by / notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|--------------------------------------|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `pointer`                            | delete      | 60+ monomorphic funcs → `func To[T any](v T) *T`, `Deref[T]`; `ToXOrNil` → one generic with `comparable`                                                                                                                                                     |
| `sort`                               | delete      | `slices.Sort`/`slices.IsSorted` (1.21); even in 2022, `sort.Slice` (1.8) covered it                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `sequence`                           | delete      | `Simple` → `for range n` (1.22); `Range` → `slices.Chunk` (1.23), and it panics on `batch == 0`; reducer → `slices.Max`/`Min` + tiny generics                                                                                                                |
| `sequence/generator`                 | delete      | `Uint32`/`Uint64` → `atomic.Uint32`/`atomic.Uint64` (1.19); `UUID` → use `google/uuid` directly (see [[#7. UUID.Next swallows randomness failures and returns a stale value]])                                                                               |
| `strings`                            | mostly del. | `Concat` → `+`/`strings.Join`; `PresentAny` → `slices.Contains`; `Exclude`/`NotEmpty` → `slices.DeleteFunc`; `FirstNotEmpty` → `cmp.Or` (1.22); keep `strings/bytes` (byte-size parsing has no stdlib home); `strings/numd` is niche — keep only if consumed |
| `unsafe`                             | delete      | `DoSilent`/`Ignore` are spelled `_ =` in idiomatic Go; `Return` → generic `Must[T]`; the name collides with built-in `unsafe`, scaring linters and readers for nothing                                                                                       |
| `pointer`, `fn`                      | shrink      | `fn.Must` is fine minus `pkg/errors`; `HasNoError`/`HoldContext`/`timer.Stopwatch` are one-liners callers can own                                                                                                                                            |
| `env`                                | delete      | `os.Environ` + `strings.Cut` (1.18); the constants are not worth an import                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `testing`                            | delete      | `t.Setenv` (1.17), `t.TempDir`, `t.Context` (1.24); see [[#4. SetEnvs holds a global mutex across the test body and deadlocks on failure]]                                                                                                                   |
| `sync`                               | shrink      | `Termination` → `signal.NotifyContext` (1.16); `Times` has no stdlib analog — keep                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `async`                              | delete      | `Job` → `errgroup.Group` (which the doc itself concedes) or `sync.WaitGroup.Go` (1.25); `Watcher` needs a rewrite either way                                                                                                                                 |
| `io`                                 | keep+fix    | `TeeReadCloser`, cascade closers, `Discarded` are genuinely useful; fix [[#1. RepeatableReadCloser treats any short read as end of stream]]; `ReadNopCloser` → `io.NopCloser` (1.16)                                                                         |
| `errors`                             | keep+fix    | `Classifier` is the one real asset; fix findings 2 and 8; `Message` (const errors) is still a good idiom                                                                                                                                                     |
| `safe`                               | keep        | Small, useful, but see [[#12. safe.Do loses the panic value and misses panic nil]]                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `encoding`, `exp`, `time`, `runtime` | delete/fold | Two-interface glue, an empty experiment, two constants, and `Version` → `go/version` (1.22) + fix [[#6. Caller resolves PCs with FuncForPC which is wrong under inlining]]                                                                                   |

**Fix.** Decide what this module *is* before modernizing it. Recommended: cut a v1 that keeps `safe`, `errors`, `io`, `sync.Times`, and `strings/bytes` (fixed and generic where sensible), deprecate the rest with pointers to stdlib equivalents, and let consumers migrate via `go fix`-style search-and-replace. Modernizing all 18 packages in place is effort spent maintaining worse spellings of the standard library.

## 12. safe.Do loses the panic value and misses panic nil

`safe/do.go:24-30, 37-39`

`recovered.Error()` returns the constant `"unexpected panic occurred"` — the actual panic value is only reachable by type-asserting to the package's `Recovered` interface, so any plain `log.Println(err)` in a handler logs a message with zero forensic content, and `errors.As`/`errors.Is` cannot see the cause either because the type has no `Unwrap`. Separately, `if r := recover(); r != nil` combined with the module's `go 1.13` directive means `panic(nil)` is swallowed entirely (the Go 1.21 `PanicNilError` behavior is disabled by the `panicnil` GODEBUG for modules declaring < 1.21): the action's panic vanishes and the handler never fires. Finally, the stack captured via `pkg/errors.WithStack` is the recovery site's stack, not the panicking goroutine's frame of failure — `debug.Stack()` inside the recover is what actually helps.

**Fix.** Format the cause into the message (`fmt.Sprintf("recovered: %v", r)`), keep `Cause`, add `Unwrap() error` when the cause is itself an error, capture `debug.Stack()` at recovery, and bump the go directive so `panic(nil)` cannot slip through (or handle it explicitly). Drop `pkg/errors`.

## 13. Package names shadow the standard library across the whole module

`unsafe/suppress.go:1` (also `strings`, `io`, `sync`, `errors`, `testing`, `time`, `sort`, `runtime`, `encoding`, `bytes`, `http`)

Twelve of the module's packages reuse a standard library package name, and one reuses the `unsafe` built-in pseudo-package. Every consumer that needs both must alias one import; goimports guesses wrong; code review readers see `sync.Times(100)` or `unsafe.Ignore(err)` and reach for the wrong docs; greps for `"io"` imports match the wrong module. `go.octolab.org/unsafe` is the worst offender — a name that triggers security-review heuristics for a package that merely discards errors. This was a known trade-off in 2019-era "extended stdlib" designs, but it aged badly and it compounds finding 8's shadowed-name confusion.

**Fix.** If a v1 reorganization happens per [[#11. Most packages are superseded by the modern standard library]], take the opportunity to rename the survivors (`safe` is already fine; `errors` → `errclass` or similar; `io` extras → `ioext`; retire `unsafe` entirely). For any package kept under its stdlib name, at least document the intended import alias in the package comment.
